newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece signals diplomatic attack against Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Greece signals diplomatic attack against Turkey.

text.p: Greek Socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis vowed on Thursday to launch a diplomatic offensive against Turkey in his first major policy speech after winning elections last month.
Simitis told parliament, where he is seeking a confidence vote this week, that Greece would fend off what it sees as Turkish aggression with an intensified diplomatic effort.
"We will support peace in the area but our policy will combine diplomatic quickening with deterrence ability," he said.
"Our multi-faceted diplomatic campaign has created problems for Turkey in the past few months with those who had a neutrality favourable for Turkey," he said. "We will continue."

The two neighbouring Balkan countries are at odds over a number of territorial and minority issues and the divided island of Cyprus. U.S. intervention stopped their fleets from clashing over a deserted islet in the Aegean in January.

Simitis, 60, who had a strong election win on September 22, painted fellow NATO member Turkey as an aggressor who destabilised the whole region and urged Ankara to take its case to the International Court at The Hague.

"Present Turkish policy is not only dangerous for Greece but for the security and balance in the Eastern Mediterranean and that is starting to be understood by an increasing number of countries," he said.
He rejected Ankara's repeated calls for a dialogue to sort out differences saying Greece would never sit down to negotiate its borders.

But he stopped short of flexing any military muscles, avoiding specific pledges of new arms purchases and stressing that Greece would be strong only if it was brought up to speed with its European Union partners.
The EU's poorest member, Greece faces chronic state deficits and high inflation that have crippled its economic development.

Simitis, who made clear during his election campaign that hard work was ahead to bring the ailing ecomomy around, said his immediate targets were cutting state spending and collecting "We can change the face of Greece," he said. "This is the most critical period, one which will decide whether we actively participate in international developments or slip towards marginalisation and isolation."
A mild-mannered economist, Simitis succeeded in January his flamboyant mentor, the late socialist leader Andreas Papandreou, who died in June.
He has a comfortable 162-seat majority in the 300-set parliament and is expected to easily win the Saturday midnight confidence vote.
